title: Duo in the Dark
caption: Two ALMA antennas beneath Orion, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) stand together on the Chajnantor Plateau on a winter night. Above them hangs the constellation of Orion, the Hunter, recognisable by his starry belt, with the red supergiant Betelgeuse marking his shoulder on the right of the photo.

These are two of the 66 antennas that make up ALMA, in which ESO is a partner. They observe in millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which are hard to catch from the ground because water vapour in the atmosphere absorbs them. Telescopes working in this light must sit very high, where the air is drier. ALMA's antennas therefore stand at 5000 metres.
Betelgeuse lies just under 650 light-years from us. It is a prime target for ALMA's kind of observations, as is the nearby Orion Nebula.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so faint stars appear brighter and more numerous than they would to someone standing there.

explore: The plateau can feel very isolated on winter nights, but it offers some of the driest and darkest skies anywhere, which is exactly what ALMA needs to work well, and conditions worth sharing with others.
alt: Two dish antennas under a night sky, with the constellation Orion above them and a reddish star on the right.
